fit: clove exposure and Parkinson fall frequency
assessment: The review describes antimicrobial studies using cinnamon and clove oils, including combinations, and intestinal experiments that assess clove preparations. These results do not supply an evaluation of eating ground clove for Parkinson falls.

fit: cumin exposure and Parkinson anxiety severity
assessment: The review cites a laboratory report that extracts safranal from cumin seed and discusses anxiety-related models elsewhere for safranal. It does not connect toasted cumin and a clinical anxiety measurement.

fit: canola oil exposure and Parkinson pain severity
assessment: An included study compares olive and canola oil in broiler feed and measures performance and immune outcomes. It supplies no evidence from cold-pressed canola consumed by people with Parkinson disease for pain.

fit: dark chocolate exposure and Parkinson anxiety severity
assessment: The case-report review documents anxiety in 16 and tremor in 14 of the 89 cases with details on initial presentation or laboratory results. A separate table provides a typical caffeine-content estimate for dark chocolate. These datasets do not yield a dark chocolate anxiety estimate or address dried date fruit.

fit: fig extract toxicity surveillance in healthy rats
assessment: Tremor was on the toxicity checklist. Table 4 presents no separate event count or rest-tremor score. Exposure and dose units vary in the reporting.

fit: date fruit and premenstrual abdominal-cramp outcomes
assessment: The original abstract claims improvement and gives a hormone association, without a between-arm estimate of cramp severity or dry preparation details.

fit: oral cinnamon powder and pain severity during dysmenorrhea
assessment: Table 2 gives cinnamon versus empty capsule means of 5.2 vs 6.3, 5.7 vs 6.1 and 5.4 vs 6.3. Corrected counts and unblinded self-reports limit transfer to Parkinson disease.

fit: fig and olive oil in customary bowel and pain uses
assessment: Local interviews and a separate historical source report customary uses of fig and olive oil. No grade, differential exposure or controlled clinical constipation severity was measured.
